notes.meaning: Saul drops his secret plotting and openly tells Jonathan and his officers to put David to death. Jonathan, however, was deeply attached to David as his dear friend. Saul probably hoped Jonathan would put his own royal inheritance ahead of his friendship, but Jonathan chose loyalty to God and David instead.

Jonathan quickly warns David about his father's deadly plan. He tells David to hide in a secret spot in the morning until he can find out what Saul intends to do. True friendship means protecting others from harm, even at great personal risk.

Jonathan plans to walk with his father in the open field near David's hiding place. That way, he can speak up for David, listen to Saul's response, and safely report back. This careful plan gave David a chance to hear or quickly learn how dangerous the king still was.

Jonathan speaks up for David with great respect and courage before the king. He reminds Saul that David has never wronged him, but has only done things that brought great good to the kingdom. A good friend defends the innocent when others falsely accuse them.

Jonathan points out that David risked his life when he fought Goliath, and the Lord won a huge victory for all Israel through him. Saul had celebrated that day, so Jonathan asks why he would now kill an innocent man without any cause. Remembering past blessings helps calm our anger and jealousy toward others.

Saul is moved by Jonathan's truthful appeal and takes a solemn vow before God not to kill David. For a moment, Saul genuinely felt convicted and changed his mind. Yet his quick promise shows how easily feelings can change without lasting heart change.

Jonathan calls David out of hiding and tells him all about his father's oath. Then he brings David back to Saul's court, where David returns to serving the king just as before. This shows David's humility and willingness to forgive and serve even after being threatened.

A new war breaks out with the Philistines, and David leads his soldiers to another crushing victory. David's military success makes him even more popular among the people. Even when David faithfully did his duty, it ended up stirring Saul's jealousy all over again.

Saul's dark mood and jealousy return while he sits in his palace holding his spear. God permitted a troubling spirit to torment Saul because the king had turned his back on the Lord. Even though Saul was dangerous, David humbly returned to play the harp to soothe him.

In a sudden burst of rage, Saul hurls his spear at David, trying to pin him to the wall. David dodges just in time, and the spear sinks deep into the wall while David escapes into the night. God protected David's life through his quickness, ending David's days in Saul's royal court.

Saul sends royal guards to watch David's house all night so they can kill him when he comes out in the morning. David's wife Michal learns of the plot and warns him that he will be dead by dawn if he does not flee immediately. God often provides escape through the watchfulness of family and friends.

Michal helps David escape by lowering him out of a back window, away from the guards watching the doors. David runs into the dark and safely gets away. This nighttime escape marked the start of David's long years on the run as a fugitive.

To buy David more time, Michal takes a household idol, places it on the bed, and covers it with a blanket. She places goat hair near the top to look like a man's hair in the dim bedroom light. These idols were common pagan statues that should not have been kept in an Israelite home.

When Saul's soldiers come to seize David, Michal tells them that her husband is sick in bed. Her trick gave David hours to put distance between himself and the palace guards. While her loyalty helped save David, her lie showed she relied on human tricks rather than trusting God alone.

Saul refuses to let illness stop him, ordering the guards to carry David in his entire bed so he can kill him personally. Saul's fierce hatred had made him completely blind to justice and basic mercy. His command revealed how desperate he was to destroy his rival with his own hands.

The messengers enter the bedchamber and discover they have been completely fooled by an idol with goat hair. The trick gave David the head start he needed to reach safety. God used even this clever decoy to frustrate the plans of wicked men.

Saul angrily confronts Michal for betraying him and helping his enemy escape. Michal defends herself with another lie, claiming David had threatened to kill her if she did not help him. Saul calls David his enemy, though David had never done anything but help and serve him.

David flees to Ramah to seek out Samuel, the prophet who had first anointed him as king. David tells Samuel everything Saul had done, seeking comfort and spiritual guidance in his distress. Samuel then takes David to Naioth, a place near Ramah where prophets lived and studied together.

Word quickly reaches Saul that David is staying at Naioth in Ramah. Even though David had sought shelter in a sacred place of worship and study, Saul's anger was not restrained. When bitterness takes over a person's heart, even holy places will not stop them from doing wrong.

Saul sends a group of soldiers to capture David at the prophetic settlement. When the men arrive and see Samuel leading the prophets in praising God, the Spirit of God comes upon the soldiers, and they begin prophesying too. God stopped the armed men in their tracks by filling them with His praise instead of violence.

When Saul hears what happened, he sends a second group of soldiers, and then a third, but the exact same thing happens to each group. Every time Saul sends men to arrest David, God's Spirit captures the men instead. Human power cannot fight against the plans and Spirit of God.

Refusing to give up, Saul heads to Ramah himself to finish the job. He stops at the great cistern at Secu to ask where Samuel and David are, and the locals point him to Naioth. Saul's stubborn march shows how blindly a person can pursue sin even after God has repeatedly blocked the way.

As Saul walks along toward Naioth, the Spirit of God comes upon him before he even arrives. He begins speaking praises and prophesying all the way to the town. God showed Saul that the king was completely powerless against the Lord's chosen servant.

At Naioth, Saul strips off his royal robes and lies on the ground all day and night in an ecstatic trance before Samuel. God humbled the proud king by taking away his royal dignity, reminding everyone that Saul had been stripped of his kingdom. This event renewed the famous saying, 'Is Saul also among the prophets?'
